It seems like it used to be that anyone who did partial reps was just a cheater trying to satisfy their ego. Then some big names came out in favor of them, and now there's lots of people saying they build more strength with partial reps than they would without them. And then of course there's the people who never let go of the idea that they're simply cheaters with big egos to satisfy, And the battle continues.

Personally I feel that partial reps are a good once-in-a-while variety technique to shake things up and use more weight and put more stress on the muscles, thus really overloading your body. And if you're stuck in a plateau, partial reps are one of the better ways to break out of it.

But I also feel like alot of people use partial reps way more than they should, past me being one of them, and that there are certain risks that come along with that. The obvious one being that, yeah, you'll think you're way stronger than you are. But that's not the biggest danger, not the one I'm going to talk about, no sir.

The real danger of using partial reps is getting too strong, yes too strong, in a limited range of motion. And before anyone says that strength in range of motions is broscience, check out this study done on isometrics, I think you'll find it proves that idea wrong.

Getting too strong in a partial range of motion can have devastating effects on your performance later on down the road, when you eventually want or need that strength throughout the entire range of motion. By getting too strong in part of the motion by training with partial reps over weeks and months, you risk making it far harder to get stronger in the rest of that motion than it would otherwise be. I believe that by training only in a part of the range of motion, you convince your body that you'll never need the strength outside of it, and that there is thus some sort of strength-limiting effect outside of your comfort zone. I can't say how or why this phenomena exists, but I can say with relative certainty that it is there.

Of course, this effect is most obvious in long-time partial reppers, who may possess gorilla-like strength while doing quarter-reps, but more, ahem, kitten-like strength throughout the rest of the movement. However, I believe it can also manifest in those who do partial reps only half of the time, or even less, perhaps a quarter of the time, even. Thus I believe this advice is sound for anyone who practices partial reps at all, and if we're honest, that is most of us.

Now, perhaps the obvious thing to say is "just stop doing partial reps, dumbass!". But that's not my advice. There are always going to be those who love working partial reps, regardless of whether it is truly good for them or not. And the advice is not, "do partial reps for the other part of the exercise too!". That would just be inconvenient, and they'd be unlikely to do it. Besides, it's not even necessary, because you can keep your strength from becoming uneven with a far simpler and less time consuming technique.

That technique is this- whenever you do partial reps, end every set with a slow eccentric, all the way to the bottom of the movement, and focus on really squeezing at about halfway through the unworked ROM. Doing partial presses or handstand pushups? Eccentric all the way to the bottom, every set. Try to hold perfectly still for a second or two about 3/4s of the way down, regardless of whether you actually can or not. Doing partial pullups or one arm pullups? Jump to the top and do a slow eccentric after every set, and try to hold at just below the top for a second or two. Doing partial squats? Well, that might be a problem, depending on what equipment you have, but try to only do them when you have the necessary gear to do controlled eccentrics safely. [Note- if you do pistol squats, even weighted ones, this problem goes away].

So there you have it. Maybe one day we can all be saints and only do full ROM, or maybe we can become enlightened and only do partial reps with the goal of eventually expanding them and working towards full ROM at that particular level. But until that day comes, and I know that for a lot of us it never will, use this technique, and don't become one of those half-gorilla-half-kittens we all know one or two of.
